item.title: AI Models Help Independent Researchers Identify New Exoplanet Candidates
item.description:
AI Models Help Independent Researchers Identify New Exoplanet Candidates

Independent researchers have used AI coding and analysis tools to identify new planetary signals in data from NASA’s Kepler and TESS missions, contributing to the growing catalog of over 6,400 confirmed exoplanets.

🧩 How it works

Two independent efforts leveraged AI to process large datasets:

  • Kevin Bond used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope. Codex compared different search methods, combined them into a single program, and tested code changes to improve results. When run on public Kepler data, the program flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets.
  • Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, used a model called Astra to design two searches analyzing data from TESS and other public telescope archives. His searches identified 49 candidates in the first pass.

⚙️ Key details

The search produced specific planetary candidates that are now undergoing independent verification:

Star Signal Period Estimated Size/Type Notes
KIC 5689121 13.8 days ~2.4x Earth’s diameter Cool star, half the size of the sun, in Lyra
KIC 6691030 4.8 days Smaller than Neptune Faint star in the northern sky

An astronomer at the SETI Institute independently found two signals in the Kepler data that matched Bond’s findings. Byrd has sent one of his strongest TESS candidates to NASA researchers for further analysis, with two more candidates awaiting submission.

💡 Why it matters

The 2017 success of neural networks finding an eighth planet orbiting Kepler-90 set a precedent for AI-assisted astronomy. These new efforts extend that approach, using large language models to write and optimize code that sifting through millions of stellar observations to find previously hidden planetary transits.

#Exoplanets #Astronomy #GenerativeAI #NASA #DataScience

Source: Searching for distant planets with Astra

item.title: New TACLS Software Uses Machine Learning to Improve Flash Flood Alerts
item.description:
New TACLS Software Uses Machine Learning to Improve Flash Flood Alerts

Scientists from UCSD, the NWS, and NASA have collaborated to create the Transient Artifact and Continuous Learning System (TACLS), a new software designed to help the National Weather Service (NWS) identify areas at risk of flash flooding more quickly.

🧩 How it works

TACLS utilizes a combination of satellites and machine learning to identify specific locations on a map that risk transitioning from rain to dangerous flash floods. This system aims to assist the 122 NWS weather forecast offices throughout the US and its territories in making better decisions when issuing flash flood alerts.

⚙️ Key details

NWS offices currently track storms using weather radars and satellites, and rely on stream and rain gauges to monitor water levels. However, these systems face certain limitations:

  • Deserts and less populated areas typically have fewer rain gauges.
  • NWS satellites provide more detail over oceans than over land.

💡 Why it matters

Floods are the deadliest type of weather event globally and the second-deadliest in the United States. The danger is significant based on water depth:

  • 6 inches: Can knock an adult off their feet.
  • 12 inches: Can lift a car.
  • 2 feet: Can move larger vehicles such as SUVs and trucks.

The NWS distinguishes a flash flood from a regular flood based on time; if an area floods in under six hours, it is classified as a flash flood.

⚠️ Alert Levels

Alert Type Severity Description
Watch Least serious Issued 12 to 48 hours in advance
Advisory Moderate Nuisance-level flooding that does not threaten life or property
Warning Most serious Highest level of alert

🚀 Availability

TACLS is currently used to identify risk areas in California, but the technology will soon be available to every NWS office.

#MachineLearning #NWS #NASA #FloodPrediction #PublicSafety

Source: Flash floods can strike without warning — this new technology could change that
